newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: SKorea offers help to North in exchange for change.
newsitem.headline: SKorea offers help to North in exchange for change.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Friday offered economic and diplomatic aid to rescue North Korea from economic ruin but said Pyongyang must first change its war-like stance toward the South.

"If North Korea chooses the path of change, we have the will and capability to cooperate with it as much as it wants," Kim said in a speech marking the 52nd anniversary of Korea's independence from 35 years of Japanese colonial rule.
Kim called the liberation of the peninsula in 1945 only partial given that Korea was divided by the victors of World War Two into the communist North and capitalist South.
He said although there had been setbacks, relations between the two Koreas were "clearly making progress", which he hoped would lead to reunification of the peninsula.
"The time has come when the South and the North should clearly perceive the true meaning of peace and work to realise it. Peace, above all, means the renunciation of arms," he said.
"North Korea has to completely give up not only the military provocations which are criminal acts against the people but also its policy of communising the South by force."

The South Korean president noted that the two Koreas, along with the United States and China, held four-nation talks in New York last week to arrange formal negotiations aimed at forging a permanent peace mechanism on the Korean peninsula.
Senior officials from the four countries failed to set an agenda for the formal peace talks but agreed to try again on September 15 in New York.

Kim said Seoul would help Pyongyang improve ties with its allies. "Of course, this has to be preceded by a change in North Korea's attitude: it must behave reasonably as a responsible member of the international community."

North Korea watchers in Seoul have said Pyongyang appeared to see better ties with Washington as a way out of the disaster that its economy has become. U.S. sanctions bar investment and trade with the reclusive North.
But Kim said on Friday: "The only ones that can extend practical help to North Korea are their brothers and sisters in the South. The North Korean authorities should accept this fact."
He said South Korea has provided 230 billion won ($257 million) worth of food to the North since 1995 when devastating floods began deepening a food shortage crisis there.
Seoul officials said international relief efforts only amounted to "stop-gap" aid as the North's famine stemmed from chronic, structural problems.
"The difficulties North Korea is facing cannot be basically resolved with temporary aid. We want to find and execute real measures to relieve North Korea from the present difficulties," Kim said.
He said Pyongyang leaders must try to help themselves. "First of all, they should free their citizens from hunger by rationally distributing their resources," he added.
South Korean officials argue that about a quarter of the North's gross national product has been used to finance its 1.1 million-strong army, one of the world's largest.
They also accuse Pyongyang of spending about $900 million annually to deify its leader Kim Jong-il and his late father, "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung.

"If it cuts five percent of its defence spendings or saves a third of its lavish propaganda expenditure, it could buy two million tonnes of food and end the food shortage," said Kim Woo-suk, Seoul's vice national unification minister.
